name: Aphids
description: Small sap-sucking insects that leave sticky honeydew on the plant.
advice: Ladybird beetles and lacewings are common predators of aphids, so please spare them when you treat.
source: NSW Department of Primary Industries, Citrus pests and their natural enemies

name: Soft scale
description: Sap-sucking insects that leave sticky honeydew on the plant.
advice: Ladybird beetles and lacewings prey on soft scales, so please spare them when you treat.
source: NSW Department of Primary Industries, Citrus pests and their natural enemies

name: Mealybugs
description: Sap-sucking insects that leave sticky honeydew on the plant.
advice: Ladybird beetles and lacewings prey on mealybugs, so please spare them when you treat.
source: NSW Department of Primary Industries, Citrus pests and their natural enemies

name: Whitefly
description: Greenhouse and silverleaf whiteflies are common pests of plants grown under cover.
advice: Parasitic wasps such as Encarsia formosa are used to control whitefly.
source: NSW Department of Primary Industries, Primefact 1007: Whitefly management in greenhouse vegetable crops

name: Two-spotted mite
description: Tiny mites that feed on a very wide range of plants. Leaves look stippled and turn yellow or bronze, and outbreaks are worse in hot, dry weather.
advice: Broad-spectrum insecticides kill the mites' predators and can make an outbreak worse. Predatory mites such as Phytoseiulus persimilis are sold in Australia.

name: Citrus leafminer
description: A pest of citrus that attacks only the new flush of leaves, mostly in late summer and autumn.
advice: On a home garden tree, pruning off the infested late summer and autumn flush helps. Horticultural mineral oils work about as well as stronger sprays, and broad-spectrum insecticides harm the leafminer's natural enemies.
source: NSW Department of Primary Industries, Citrus leafminer

name: Snails
description: Snails feed at night, in the early morning and in rainy, overcast weather.
advice: A wooden board laid under a plant shows how many snails there are, because they shelter beneath it.
source: NSW Department of Primary Industries, Snails (citrus integrated pest and disease management)

name: Powdery mildew
description: A fungal disease that shows as white, powdery patches on leaves, which spread and join up. Leaf edges may curl upwards, and purple to reddish blotches can form. It is favoured by dry weather with high humidity at about 15 to 27 °C, and its spores travel far on the wind.
advice: Check plants often and remove infected fruit, which cuts the spores that spread the disease.

name: Downy mildew
description: A disease that shows as white, downy growth on the underside of leaves in moist weather. The spots turn brown and parts of the leaf die. Warm, moist weather favours it, and low, shaded leaves that stay wet are worst affected. It affects cucurbits, grapes, lettuce and onions.
advice: Grow resistant varieties, space plants widely so air moves between them, and dig in old crops as soon as they are finished, letting them break down before planting again.

name: Grey mould (botrytis)
description: A fungal disease, mainly Botrytis cinerea, that infects ageing petals and then rots fruit, which turns soft and is soon covered in thick grey mould. It can also spot leaves and rot stems. Cool weather with heavy dew or fog favours it. Tomatoes, beans, capsicums, cucumbers, lettuce, grapes and strawberries are among its hosts.
advice: Remove diseased fruit and destroy the old crop after harvest, and keep the air drier where plants grow under cover.

name: Anthracnose
description: A fungal disease that makes dark, sunken spots, often with a raised rim, on leaves, stems and fruit, with pink spore masses and later black dots. Fruit infected before picking can rot afterwards. Wet or humid weather favours it, especially while new growth is coming, and water droplets spread it. Tomatoes, capsicums, citrus, mangoes, avocados, passionfruit and bananas are among its hosts.
advice: Prune out dead wood before flowering, remove infected fruit and dead leaves, keep the canopy open, and do not save seed from infected plants.

name: Late blight
description: A disease of potatoes and tomatoes that makes large, pale green, water-soaked patches on leaves, which darken and spread quickly, with white fluffy growth underneath in humid weather. Tomato fruit gets firm, dark brown patches. Wet, humid weather at about 21 °C favours it, and its spores travel on rain splash and wind.
advice: Late blight is a declared pest in Western Australia, so please report it to the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development if you see it there.
source: Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (WA), Late blight of potato and tomato

name: Myrtle rust
description: A rust of the myrtle family, such as lilly pillies, willow myrtle, bottlebrushes, paperbarks and tea-trees. It shows as golden-yellow spore masses and purple or brown spots on young leaves near the tips, which may curl or dry out, and growing tips can wither. Warm, humid weather with leaves wet for six hours or more favours it.
advice: Avoid touching the spores, prune off affected parts or remove badly affected plants, and bag the material for household rubbish, not green waste or compost. In Tasmania a home garden case need not be reported, but one in native forest must be.
source: Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania, Myrtle rust
